chapters.title: Chapter 4: Valuing Stocks Across the Cycle

lessons.title: Price to Book, EV/EBITDA, and Replacement Cost for Cyclicals

body.text: Earnings are the least stable thing about a cyclical. Its assets, its debt, and what it would cost to rebuild its plants are far steadier. Value the steady things, and you get a much clearer read on whether a cyclical is cheap or expensive.

children.text: Normalised earnings fix the P/E by replacing this year's profit with a typical year's. Specialists in metals, cement, and other capital-heavy businesses also lean on three tools that avoid volatile earnings altogether, or at least handle debt properly. This lesson covers price to book, EV/EBITDA, and replacement cost, tests the first two on Tata Steel, and shows what each one hides.

cells: Share price with net assets per share
Book value moves slowly, so the ratio does not swing with one year's profit
Book value can be distorted by impairments, old asset costs, and equity raises
Value of the whole business, including debt, with operating profit before depreciation and interest
Captures debt, which drives cyclical risk, and compares companies with different leverage fairly
Uses current EBITDA, so it suffers the same peak and trough distortion as P/E
Enterprise value per tonne of capacity with the cost of building new capacity
Links valuation to the supply cycle: cheap capacity discourages new building
Capacity estimates and construction costs vary widely by location and technology

markDefs.definition: Shareholders' equity, meaning equity capital plus reserves, divided by the number of shares. It represents the accounting value of net assets belonging to each share.

children.text: A steel company's profit can swing from a loss to a record in two years, but its

changes slowly, because it accumulates profits and losses over many years. That makes P/B a steadier yardstick. It also has an intuitive meaning for capital-heavy businesses: a P/B below 1 means the market values the company at less than the accounting value of its plants, mines, and working capital, net of debt.

body.latex: \text{P/B} = \frac{\text{Share price}}{\text{Book value per share}} \qquad \text{Justified P/B} = \frac{\text{ROE} - g}{r - g}
body.caption: ROE = return on equity, g = long-term growth, r = required return. A company earning exactly its required return deserves a P/B of about 1.

children.text: The justified P/B formula connects this tool back to normalised earnings. What deserves a premium to book is not this year's ROE but the ROE the business can earn across a cycle. A steel maker with a 25% ROE in a boom year and a 5% ROE in a bust is really a 12% to 14% ROE business, and should be judged on that.

body.caption: Tata Steel at end-July each year: P/B, EV/EBITDA, and the next year's price change (split-adjusted, price only)

body.title: Tata Steel Price to Book at End-July

children.text: P/B behaves more sensibly than the P/E did in the last lesson. In the four years when Tata Steel traded below 0.8 times book, 2015, 2016, 2019, and 2020, the price rose over the following year three times, including the near-quadrupling from July 2020. In July 2021, at 2.31 times book near the height of the boom, the price fell 25% over the next year. P/B did not flash 'cheap' at the 2022 earnings peak the way the P/E of 3.3 did, because a single record year barely moves book value.

body.text: P/B is steadier, not foolproof. July 2019 was cheap at 0.72 times book and still fell 15.2% the next year before soaring. Book value itself also moves for reasons unrelated to the cycle: Tata Steel's book value per share fell from ₹84.4 in March 2023 to ₹73.8 in March 2024 largely because of UK impairments, and rights issues in earlier years added shares. A write-down shrinks book value and makes P/B look higher without the price changing. And P/B has risen above 2 in recent years partly because impairments reduced book value, so compare it with the business's normalised ROE, not just its own history.

body.title: Why Is Book Value Steadier?
body.question: In FY22, Tata Steel's consolidated net profit jumped more than five times. Its P/E fell to 3.3 by July 2022, but its P/B was a moderate 1.15. Why did P/B move so much less?
options: Book value is not affected by profits
Book value accumulates a company's entire history of retained profits and losses, so one exceptional year changes it only partly
Tata Steel issued a large number of new shares in FY22
P/B uses the next year's forecast book value
body.explanation: P/E divides by one year's earnings, so one boom year changes the denominator enormously. Book value adds each year's retained profit to decades of accumulated equity, so even a record year moves it by a fraction. That stability is exactly why P/B is favoured for cyclicals and banks.

markDefs.definition: Enterprise value: market capitalisation plus debt minus cash. It represents the value of the whole business to all its capital providers, shareholders and lenders together.

children.text: Chapter 2 showed that debt is what turns a cyclical downturn into a crisis. P/E and P/B look only at shareholders.

adds the lenders. Dividing EV by EBITDA, operating profit before depreciation, interest, and tax, tells you how many years of operating profit the whole business is priced at, regardless of how it is financed.

body.caption: Screener.in's Operating Profit line is a close proxy for EBITDA

body.title: Why EV matters: two companies, same market cap

children.text: Both companies look equally valued if you only check market cap. But Company B's buyer is also taking on ₹18,000 crore of debt that has to be serviced through every downturn. Per rupee of operating profit, Company B is about 73% more expensive, and it carries far more financial leverage into the next bust.

children.text: EV/EBITDA handles debt properly but inherits the P/E paradox, because EBITDA also peaks and troughs with the cycle. Tata Steel's EV/EBITDA of 30.4 in July 2015 and 3.3 in July 2022 pointed in exactly the wrong directions. The fix is the same as last lesson: use mid-cycle EBITDA. Applying the 13.1% average margin to FY26 revenue gives mid-cycle EBITDA of about ₹30,333 crore and an EV/EBITDA of about 10.8 in July 2026, compared with 9.6 on actual FY26 EBITDA.

body.title: What EV Adds
body.textWithBlank: Unlike market capitalisation, enterprise value includes a company's ___, which is why EV/EBITDA is better suited to comparing highly leveraged cyclicals.
body.explanation: EV adds debt and subtracts cash, so two companies with the same market cap but very different borrowings show very different valuations, reflecting the extra risk that debt brings into a downturn.

markDefs.definition: The cost of building equivalent new production capacity today, usually expressed per tonne of annual capacity for cement and steel.

children.text: The last tool connects valuation directly to the supply cycle from Chapter 2. Divide a company's EV by its annual production capacity and you get what the market is paying for each tonne of capacity. Compare that with the

of building a new tonne. When existing capacity trades well below what it costs to build, no rational company builds new plants; it buys existing ones. Supply stops growing, which eventually supports prices. When capacity trades well above replacement cost, everyone rushes to build, and the next oversupply begins.

body.caption: ₹1 crore per million tonnes of capacity equals ₹100 per tonne

children.text: Notice the gap between the two industries: a tonne of steel capacity costs more than ten times a tonne of cement capacity. That is why steel is more capital-intensive, carries more depreciation and debt, and swings harder. It also shows why replacement cost comparisons must stay within one industry, and ideally within one region and technology.

body.title: Price the Capacity
body.prompt: A cement company has an enterprise value of ₹15,000 crore and installed capacity of 30 million tonnes a year. What is its EV per tonne of capacity, in rupees?
body.explanation: ₹15,000 crore ÷ 30 million tonnes = ₹500 crore per million tonnes = ₹5,000 per tonne. If building a comparable new greenfield plant in its region costs, say, ₹7,500 per tonne, the market is valuing its existing capacity at about two thirds of replacement cost, a signal worth investigating rather than a buy signal on its own.

body.title: Buy or Build?
body.scenario: A large cement maker announces it will acquire a struggling regional rival. The deal values the rival at an EV of about ₹6,000 per tonne of capacity. Industry sources estimate a new greenfield plant in that region would cost around ₹8,000 per tonne and take three to four years to build. Cement prices in the region have been weak for two years, and two smaller players have delayed expansion plans.
body.prompt: What does this deal tell you about where the regional cement cycle might be, and what should an investor in the listed acquirer check?
body.modelAnswer: Buying capacity at about 75% of replacement cost, with no construction delay, is a classic late-downturn signal. When distressed capacity sells below what it costs to build, new supply tends to be delayed, as the two smaller players' decisions suggest, and consolidation improves pricing discipline. That can set up the next upcycle. But it is a signal, not a certainty. An investor in the acquirer should check: whether the acquired plants are efficient or need heavy spending to modernise, which would raise the true cost per tonne; how the deal is funded, since adding debt in a weak market increases financial leverage; how much other capacity is still under construction in the region; and whether the acquirer's own balance sheet can absorb a longer downturn if prices stay weak.

body.label: Use them together
body.value: No single ratio values a cyclical reliably
body.context: Normalised P/E, P/B against normalised ROE, mid-cycle EV/EBITDA, and EV per tonne against replacement cost each catch mistakes the others miss

body.title: Your Cyclical Valuation Toolkit
steps: Calculate P/E on normalised earnings from the previous lesson
Note Book Value from Screener.in's top ratios and calculate P/B; compare it with the stock's own history and with its normalised ROE
Check whether recent impairments, write-downs, or equity raises have distorted book value
Calculate EV as market cap plus borrowings minus cash, then EV/EBITDA on both actual and mid-cycle EBITDA
From the annual report or investor presentation, find installed capacity and calculate EV per tonne
Compare EV per tonne with recent acquisition prices and announced capex per tonne in the same industry and region
Write down where all four measures agree and where they conflict, and what would explain the difference

points: P/B is steadier than P/E for cyclicals because book value accumulates many years of profits and losses
At Tata Steel, P/B below 0.8 was followed by price gains in three of four years, while P/B above 2.3 in 2021 preceded a 25% fall
Impairments and equity raises can distort book value, so judge P/B against normalised ROE, not just history
EV/EBITDA includes debt, making it essential for comparing leveraged cyclicals, but it needs mid-cycle EBITDA to avoid the P/E paradox
EV per tonne below replacement cost discourages new capacity and often signals a late-downturn phase of the supply cycle
Steel capacity costs more than ten times cement capacity per tonne, so replacement cost comparisons must stay within one industry

body.text: Tata Steel book value per share uses consolidated equity capital plus reserves at 31 March of each year from Screener.in, with share counts adjusted for the 2022 split. EV is simplified as market capitalisation plus gross borrowings, without deducting cash, and EBITDA is Screener.in's operating profit, so the ratios are approximate. Prices are split-adjusted closes from historical market data; returns exclude dividends. Capex figures are derived from reported announcements and are not like-for-like benchmarks. Company A, Company B, the cement examples, and the scenario are illustrative. This lesson is educational and not a recommendation to buy or sell any security.
